title: 06. Memory, State & HITL: LangChain / LangGraph Checkpointers: Complete Explanations and Examples 4/4: Operational measurements worth collec
summary: Scenario: a user double-clicks Send while a worker is still processing the previous message.

sections.title: Example 2 — Two requests arrive for the same conversation
sections.body:
**Scenario:** a user double-clicks Send while a worker is still processing the
previous message.

A connection pool can safely serve many database operations but cannot infer the
desired order of two business turns. Choose a policy: queue the second request,
reject it as busy, or intentionally create a branch. Serialize whole graph runs
for a thread, not just individual SQL inserts.

For one process, an `asyncio.Lock` keyed by thread can demonstrate the policy.
For multiple processes, that lock is insufficient. Use a shared work queue,
database-backed coordination, or the hosting platform's run-concurrency policy.
If using expiring leases, handle lease renewal and stale workers; an expired
worker must not keep writing after another worker takes ownership.

Request idempotency is separate. Give each logical input a stable request ID and
record whether it has been accepted/completed. Replaying the same HTTP request
with a new message ID can append a duplicate even if your checkpoint storage has
perfect SQL uniqueness constraints.

**Expected behavior:** two different threads can proceed independently; two
inputs to the same thread follow the application's explicit ordering policy;
duplicate delivery of one input does not create a second logical turn.

sections.title: Example 3 — Upgrade state, delete expired threads, and restore backups
sections.body:
**Scenario:** version 1 saved `customer_name`; version 2 adds `customer_id` and
renames a pending node.

Track an application state-schema version independently of the checkpoint
format's `v`. Add backward-compatible defaults when possible. A node reading
`state.get('customer_id')` can tolerate old snapshots until enrichment occurs.
Changing a field type, a reducer, a message format or a suspended node name can
break old threads even if the database tables are unchanged.

Test an actual persisted v1 fixture with v2 graph code. For incompatible graph
changes, drain old threads with the old graph, route by graph version, or migrate
through supported state operations with a defined execution position. Do not
silently edit binary payloads while processes are writing to them. Graph
migration behavior is discussed in the
[Graph API guide](https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langgraph/graph-api#graph-migrations).

For retention, classify active, suspended and completed threads. Do not expire
pending approvals before the promised response window. Prefer whole-thread
deletion when that matches the policy. Selective pruning must understand blob
references, pending writes, forks and delta ancestor dependencies. Dropping
“everything older than yesterday” can corrupt today's retained state.

A restore test should load a backed-up thread, inspect state, resume pending work,
and check that external-operation IDs still prevent duplicate effects. Back up
associated blobs/writes and maintain graph/serializer/key compatibility. Also
account for exported reporting tables, Store memories and backup retention when
implementing user-data deletion.

sections.title: Operational measurements worth collecting
sections.body: Record checkpoint write/read latency, payload sizes, database/pool wait time, failed saver operations, pending-approval age and recovery failures. Keep these metrics separate from token/LLM latency so storage bottlenecks are visible. Use checkpoint IDs in internal diagnostics, while presenting business language in the product UI.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.body:
This chapter gives three implementation designs. The MySQL/SQL Server and
DynamoDB/object-store sections are **porting blueprints, not drop-in savers**.
The Cosmos section identifies a maintained integration. These services were not
provisioned or live-tested for this course.

The critical contract is independent of SQL versus NoSQL: persist checkpoint
identity, full runtime payload, metadata, parent link, ordered task writes,
history queries and deletion. Your database must support the guarantees your
implementation promises.

sections.title: Example 1 — Port the teaching schema to MySQL or SQL Server
sections.body:
**Scenario:** your organization requires its existing relational database and
its naming standards, such as `workflow_snapshots` and `workflow_task_writes`.

Start with `custom_sqlite.py` as the behavior specification, not as a script to
run unchanged against another database. Replace the connection layer, parameter
markers, binary types, upsert syntax and transaction handling.

| Concern | MySQL design choice | SQL Server design choice |
|---|---|---|
| Schema ownership | Database/schema naming plus a controlled role | Explicit schema such as `agent_state` |
| Serialized payload | Suitable BLOB size, such as LONGBLOB | VARBINARY(MAX) |
| Identity values | Bounded, case-sensitive indexed strings | Bounded strings with deliberate collation |
| Idempotent writes | Unique key with intentional duplicate handling | Unique key with transactional insert/update logic |
| Latest/history query | Ordered indexed lookup plus LIMIT | Ordered indexed lookup plus TOP/OFFSET |
| Atomic thread delete | Transaction covering writes and snapshots | Transaction covering writes and snapshots |

Do not choose maximum-length indexed strings independently: the combined
composite key must fit the database's index constraints. If you hash a long
namespace for indexing, retain its original value and define collision checks.
Case-insensitive collation can incorrectly treat two different thread IDs as the
same identity; explicitly choose the intended comparison semantics.

Translate one method at a time:

1. `put` binds all values, stores serializer tags and blobs, and returns the new ID.
2. `get_tuple` performs exact/latest lookup and loads matching writes.
3. `put_writes` preserves the task key and reserved-write semantics.
4. `list` supports filters and pagination before imposing limits.
5. `delete_thread` removes every namespace and associated row transactionally.
6. Async variants use a suitable driver or a clearly documented adapter.

Run the same restart, parallel-failure, fork and transaction tests against the new
backend, then add database-specific concurrency tests. A community saver may
already exist; review its maintenance, version compatibility and feature tests
before deciding to own an implementation yourself.

sections.title: Example 2 — Use Azure Cosmos DB for NoSQL through its integration
sections.body:
Microsoft's `langchain-azure-cosmosdb` package provides `CosmosDBSaverSync` and
`CosmosDBSaver` for synchronous and asynchronous checkpointing. It also offers
separate Store/cache integrations. Use the correct component for graph state.
See [Microsoft's integration overview](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/cosmos-db/gen-ai/integrations).

An application rollout needs a chosen account, database and checkpoint container,
the integration's required partition-key layout, identity/credential setup,
throughput settings and retention policy. Select names through the integration's
supported constructor, but preserve its required document fields and indexes.
Do not point it at an unrelated existing business container without checking
partitioning and validation compatibility.

Use this verification sequence before connecting a real agent:

```text
construct the version-pinned saver with tutorial database/container names
compile counter_graph(saver)
invoke count 10 under a new thread ID
close client/process
construct the same saver and graph
get_state -> expect count 11
run approval, parallel failure, history and deletion checks
```

This sequence is deliberately API-neutral where package versions differ. Inspect
the installed constructor rather than inventing arguments from another Cosmos
integration. A Cosmos DB API for MongoDB endpoint and Cosmos DB for NoSQL are
different integration choices; do not mix their clients or storage assumptions.

sections.title: Example 3 — DynamoDB with optional object storage for large payloads
sections.body: **Scenario:** a custom backend wants database metadata/identity lookups and external objects for large serialized checkpoint bodies. One possible design encodes tenant, thread and namespace in a partition key; checkpoint ID is part of an ordered sort key. Task-write records include the checkpoint ID, task ID and write index. A latest-pointer item can be updated using a conditional write so competing writers do not silently overwrite ownership. Specify consistent-read behavior where an immediate resume must observe a commit. Store a serializer tag, object URI, checksum, payload size and format version in the checkpoint record. Upload the immutable object before publishing a reference to it. A failed metadata write can leave an orphan object; clean it up only after a grace period and reachability check. A metadata record must never reference an object that lifecycle expiry has already deleted. Object storage alone still needs a design for latest lookup, history ordering, atomic publication, task writes and concurrent writers. A file named `thread_id.json` overwritten on every call lacks those properties. Large-object offloading also adds another read and another operational failure point. **Expected result:** after reconnect, the saver reconstructs the same full CheckpointTuple, including pending writes. The graph should not know whether the bytes lived in a BLOB column or an object store. The backend owns that translation and its consistency guarantees.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.body:
These walkthroughs combine the earlier concepts. The executable building blocks
are the graph labs, database recipes, restart demo and audit exporter. External
model calls, payment services and deployed APIs are application-specific; the
flows below identify exactly where they fit.

sections.title: Example 1 — A RAG support assistant with conversation memory
sections.body:
**Goal:** a user asks a follow-up question after the API restarts, and the
assistant remembers the conversation while retrieving current knowledge.

Suggested state:

```python
class SupportState(MessagesState):
    question: str
    document_ids: list[str]
    document_versions: list[str]
    answer: str
```

Flow: accept new message -> derive search query -> retrieve document references
-> generate answer -> return answer. Compile once with a persistent saver. Use
one authorized thread per conversation. On the next message, send only the new
message; the graph loads previous messages. Use a separate persistent Store for
cross-conversation preferences such as language.

Checkpoint after retrieval contains selected document IDs and versions. If answer
generation fails, resuming from that point can reuse saved retrieval results
instead of repeating the entire request. If the product requires fresh retrieval
on every retry, encode that explicitly rather than assuming it happens.

Save source versions or immutable references when you need reproducibility.
Checkpointing a URL does not freeze the document at that URL. Keep large PDFs
outside graph state and reopen them by reference. Export answer summary and
citation IDs to a reporting table through the chapter 12 pattern.

**Verify:** run two turns, restart the process, run a third turn, then inspect
history. Test that two conversations remain separate and that a different user
cannot request this thread through the API.

sections.title: Example 2 — An order workflow requiring human approval
sections.body:
**Goal:** validate an order, price it, wait for review, and then request a single
charge even if a worker restarts.

Flow: validate -> calculate quote -> review interrupt -> approved/rejected branch
-> create charge intent -> reconcile payment -> publish result.

Use thread ID `order-workflow:<internal-order-id>` from an authorized application
lookup. Store `order_id`, `quote_version`, `amount`, `approval`, and
`payment_operation_id` in state. Use a stable operation ID such as
`order-7:quote-2:charge` so a deliberately revised quote does not accidentally
reuse the operation for another amount.

At review, return the quote and its version to the UI. Validate a later approval
against the current pending quote. Resume with `Command(resume=...)`. A rejection
routes to a cancellation result; an edit routes through any recalculation or
validation the business requires before charging.

The payment node records or reuses an idempotent external operation. If the
process dies after payment succeeds but before the checkpoint commit, recovery
queries that operation and avoids creating another charge. Checkpoint storage
does not reverse the original payment.

Built-in Postgres tables can live under `agent_state`; business tables such as
`sales.orders`, `sales.payment_operations` and `reporting.order_audit` keep your
chosen schema. Reuse chapter 08 for the runtime schema and chapter 12 for exports.

**Verify:** approve/reject/edit separately; resume after restart; inject a failure
after external-operation success; replay a historical pricing checkpoint without
accidentally charging again. The local course proves approval persistence and
idempotent-write behavior separately; it does not claim a real payment integration.

sections.title: Example 3 — Parallel research or batch document processing
sections.body: **Goal:** fetch several sources, retry the failed source, and preserve completed results across a workflow failure. Flow: plan -> parallel source tasks -> combine -> review/report. Use a reducer appropriate for parallel results. `operator.add` concatenates lists but does not deduplicate source IDs; an application needing unique sources should define a deterministic keyed merge or deduplicate at a separate node. The completed source tasks produce pending writes. If another task fails, resume the same thread with `None`. The `parallel_recovery` lab demonstrates one successful sibling running once while the failed sibling runs twice. Keep timeouts and explicit retry policies on unreliable external calls. Use separate thread IDs for independent jobs and a queue to regulate concurrency. Do not reuse one conversation thread for all jobs merely because one user owns them. If a subgraph is used per document, understand its persistence mode and generated namespace instead of hard-coding subgraph paths. For an audit/research comparison, fork from the checkpoint before combination and change the combination settings. Retain the original final checkpoint config so the UI can compare results. A replay may fetch new external data if it starts before retrieval; starting after retrieval reuses the stored references/results. **Verify:** fail one task, resume, compare execution counts, inspect task errors, fork the aggregate step, and confirm the old result remains addressable. Measure checkpoint size when the number of documents grows; switch to references when full content makes snapshots too large.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.body:
The Functional API uses `@entrypoint` and `@task` instead of declaring every node
and edge manually. It still uses the LangGraph persistence system. Apply a saver
to the entrypoint and supply a thread ID when invoking it. Task results can be
stored within the entrypoint's execution history; do not assume the same snapshot
count as a StateGraph with one node per function.

See the [Functional API guide](https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langgraph/functional-api)
for the execution and replay contract. The three examples below are implemented
and asserted in `advanced_labs.py:functional`.

sections.title: Example 1 — A completed task is reused when review resumes
sections.body:
```python
@task
def quote(amount):
    return amount * 2

@entrypoint(checkpointer=saver)
def reviewed_quote(amount):
    value = quote(amount).result()
    approved = interrupt({"quote": value})
    return {"quote": value, "approved": approved}
```

Invoke with 10, then resume the interrupt with `Command(resume=True)`. The
entrypoint's code is replayed, but the already completed task result is available.
The lab counts task calls and asserts that quote executes once, while the final
response is `{'quote': 20, 'approved': True}`.

Code outside tasks can execute again during replay. Keep nondeterministic work
and appropriate effect boundaries in tasks, and still use external idempotency
for the crash window before a task result is committed. Task persistence does
not create a distributed transaction with an external API.

sections.title: Example 2 — Carry a saved result into the next invocation
sections.body:
```python
@entrypoint(checkpointer=saver)
def running_total(value, *, previous):
    return (previous or 0) + value
```

Inputs 2 and 3 on one thread yield 2 and then 5. Input 3 on another thread yields
3. `previous` supplies the saved result from the earlier invocation in this
entrypoint/thread context. It is not a global variable shared by all users.

This differs from a StateGraph reducer: the entrypoint explicitly uses the
previous result in ordinary Python. Choose the API that makes your workflow's
state transitions easiest to understand.

sections.title: Example 3 — Save a different internal value from the public result
sections.body: ```python return entrypoint.final( value={"message": f"Accepted {value}"}, save=total, ) ``` The third example publicly returns an acknowledgement while retaining a running total for the next invocation. Inputs 4 and 6 return `Accepted 4` and `Accepted 6`, and the saved internal total is 10. This is useful when the caller-facing result and the continuity data have different shapes. The lab verifies this through a third invocation with input zero: its documented `previous` argument receives 10. This checks saved continuity without depending on internal checkpoint channel names. **Run:** `python advanced_labs.py functional`. ### Run the three examples with the full implementation below ```python from langgraph.func import entrypoint, task from langgraph.types import Send def functional(): # 1. Task results persist across an interrupted entrypoint's replay. calls = [] @task def quote(amount: int): calls.append(amount) return amount * 2 @entrypoint(checkpointer=InMemorySaver()) def reviewed_quote(amount: int): value = quote(amount).result() approved = interrupt({"quote": value}) return {"quote": value, "approved": approved} c = config("functional-review") assert reviewed_quote.invoke(10, c)["__interrupt__"] assert reviewed_quote.invoke(Command(resume=True), c) == {"quote": 20, "approved": True} assert calls == [10] print("1. Entrypoint resumed; completed quote task executed once.") # 2. Previous saved result supplies cross-invocation continuity. @entrypoint(checkpointer=InMemorySaver()) def running_total(value: int, *, previous: int | None): return (previous or 0) + value c = config("running-total") assert running_total.invoke(2, c) == 2 assert running_total.invoke(3, c) == 5 assert running_total.invoke(3, config("other-total")) == 3 print("2. Same-thread previous result accumulated 2 + 3 = 5.") # 3. Return a public response while saving a different internal value. seen_previous = [] @entrypoint(checkpointer=InMemorySaver()) def private_total(value: int, *, previous: int | None): seen_previous.append(previous) total = (previous or 0) + value return entrypoint.final(value={"message": f"Accepted {value}"}, save=total) c = config("private-total") assert private_total.invoke(4, c) == {"message": "Accepted 4"} assert private_total.invoke(6, c) == {"message": "Accepted 6"} print("3. Public outputs differ from the accumulated saved value (10).") assert private_total.invoke(0, c) == {"message": "Accepted 0"} assert seen_previous == [None, 4, 10] ``` ```python functional() ```

sections.title: Example 1 — Persist each loop iteration
sections.body:
A conditional edge routes `increment` back to itself while count is below 3,
then routes to `END`. Starting at 0, the saved history includes values 0, 1, 2
and 3. This illustrates that a repeated node name can execute in several
different super-steps; the checkpoint ID distinguishes those executions.

```python
builder.add_conditional_edges(
    "increment", lambda s: END if s["count"] >= 3 else "increment"
)
```

Set a reasonable `recursion_limit` in the run config to bound graph steps, but
also design an application stopping condition. Increasing the limit does not
fix a missing termination rule. A tool-using agent's repeated model/tool cycle
has similar persistence concerns: enough state must be saved to know what task
is next, not merely what the last message said.

sections.title: Example 2 — Dispatch an unknown number of tasks with Send
sections.body:
```python
def dispatch(state):
    return [Send("square", {"item": x}) for x in state["items"]]
```

The graph creates one square task for each item. A list reducer gathers the
results. Input `[2, 3, 4]` yields the values `[4, 9, 16]`; the lab compares sorted
results because the business result does not depend on presentation order.

The task identities and writes must remain distinct even though every task runs
the same node function. This is another reason a custom saver cannot key writes
only by node name. For work whose order matters, define and preserve a stable
application index and use deterministic aggregation.

Combine this pattern with the chapter 06 failure-recovery tests when adapting
it to remote document processing or multiple retrievers. The Send example itself
tests fan-out success, while the earlier parallel example tests failure recovery.

sections.title: Example 3 — Legal and finance reviews pause in parallel
sections.body:
Two nodes call `interrupt` with a reviewer label. The first invocation returns
two interrupts. Each has an ID. The application builds a response mapping:

```python
answers = {
    pause.id: "yes" if pause.value["reviewer"] == "legal" else "no"
    for pause in paused["__interrupt__"]
}
result = graph.invoke(Command(resume=answers), c)
```

The final state contains `legal:yes` and `finance:no`. Using IDs prevents the
application from assuming that list position identifies a particular reviewer.
Validate both the reviewer's authorization and that the interrupt remains pending
before accepting each response in a real API.

For a quorum workflow, add explicit aggregation logic after reviews complete.
The checkpoint stores progress, but the business rule deciding whether one
rejection blocks the process belongs to your graph.

**Run all three:** `python advanced_labs.py graphs`.

### Run the three examples with the full implementation below

```python
from langgraph.func import entrypoint, task
from langgraph.types import Send

def advanced_graphs():
    # 1. A conditional loop produces multiple resumable iteration boundaries.
    class Loop(TypedDict):
        count: int
    g = StateGraph(Loop).add_node("increment", lambda s: {"count": s["count"] + 1})
    g.add_edge(START, "increment")
    g.add_conditional_edges("increment", lambda s: END if s["count"] >= 3 else "increment")
    graph = g.compile(checkpointer=InMemorySaver())
    c = config("loop")
    assert graph.invoke({"count": 0}, {**c, "recursion_limit": 10})["count"] == 3
    values = [s.values.get("count") for s in graph.get_state_history(c)]
    assert all(x in values for x in (0, 1, 2, 3))
    print("1. Loop history contains counts 0, 1, 2 and 3.")

    # 2. Dynamic Send tasks share a reducer and can be recovered independently.
    class Batch(TypedDict):
        items: list[int]
        results: Annotated[list[int], operator.add]
    def dispatch(state):
        return [Send("square", {"item": x}) for x in state["items"]]
    g = StateGraph(Batch).add_node("square", lambda s: {"results": [s["item"] ** 2]})
    g.add_conditional_edges(START, dispatch).add_edge("square", END)
    graph = g.compile(checkpointer=InMemorySaver())
    assert sorted(graph.invoke({"items": [2, 3, 4], "results": []}, config("batch"))["results"]) == [4, 9, 16]
    print("2. Send fan-out returned squares 4, 9 and 16.")

    # 3. Two parallel human reviews are resumed by interrupt ID.
    class Reviews(TypedDict):
        decisions: Annotated[list[str], operator.add]
    def legal(_):
        return {"decisions": ["legal:" + interrupt({"reviewer": "legal"})]}
    def finance(_):
        return {"decisions": ["finance:" + interrupt({"reviewer": "finance"})]}
    g = StateGraph(Reviews).add_node("legal", legal).add_node("finance", finance)
    g.add_edge(START, "legal").add_edge(START, "finance")
    g.add_edge("legal", END).add_edge("finance", END)
    graph = g.compile(checkpointer=InMemorySaver())
    c = config("two-reviews")
    paused = graph.invoke({"decisions": []}, c)
    pauses = paused["__interrupt__"]
    assert len(pauses) == 2
    answers = {p.id: "yes" if p.value["reviewer"] == "legal" else "no" for p in pauses}
    result = graph.invoke(Command(resume=answers), c)
    assert sorted(result["decisions"]) == ["finance:no", "legal:yes"]
    print("3. Two interrupt IDs received different responses correctly.")
```

```python
advanced_graphs()
```

sections.title: Diagnose by symptom
sections.body:
| Symptom | Likely explanation | What to inspect or change |
|---|---|---|
| Checkpointer requires configurable keys | Missing thread identity | Pass `{'configurable': {'thread_id': stable_id}}` |
| Every message forgets earlier messages | Fresh thread/saver per request, or replacing state | Reuse the thread and persistent saver; inspect the messages reducer |
| SQLite file exists but state seems missing | Wrong path, namespace, or thread | Print the resolved file path and authorized config without secrets |
| `_GeneratorContextManager` lacks saver methods | `from_conn_string` was not entered | Use `with ... as saver` or `async with` for the async class |
| Database connection is closed | Graph escaped the saver lifetime | Keep connection/pool alive through the whole graph call |
| Async method raises NotImplementedError | Sync saver used with async graph API | Choose the async implementation or an explicitly supported adapter |
| Postgres relation does not exist | Missing migrations or wrong search path | Run controlled `setup()` and inspect every connection's schema |
| Postgres row access/type error | Incompatible row factory | Use psycopg `dict_row` as required by this saver |
| Custom Postgres schema is empty | Requests used a different connection configuration | Configure the schema for all pool connections and migration connections |
| Table renamed but saver fails | Built-in SQL still references its original names | Restore layout or implement/test a custom saver |
| Parallel nodes overwrite a list | No suitable reducer or wrong state update shape | Define and test the intended reducer |
| Successful sibling reruns after a recoverable failure | Lost/missing pending writes, wrong resume config | Check `put_writes`, saver durability and `invoke(None, same_thread)` |
| Email/payment repeated | Crash/replay repeated an external effect | Stable business operation ID and downstream idempotency/outbox design |
| Review never resumes | New thread or wrong continuation call | Same thread plus `Command(resume=...)` for dynamic interrupts |
| Old approval affects a new request | API did not validate pending-review identity | Match the response to the current pending operation/version |
| Replayed result differs | Nodes after the checkpoint ran again | Pin inputs/models/data where needed; replay is execution, not just reading |
| Old snapshot still contains deleted message | `RemoveMessage` changed current state only | Apply a separate historical retention/deletion policy |
| Saver list is slow | Unbounded history or unindexed metadata filter | Paginate; index supported filters; apply a valid retention strategy |
| SQLite is locked | Writer contention or long transactions | Short transactions; correct lifecycle; consider service-backed storage |
| Redis index/module error | Missing JSON/search capabilities or setup | Check server features and call the correct setup API |
| Redis data disappears unexpectedly | TTL, eviction, lost server persistence | Check all three; a saver does not configure Redis durability |
| MongoDB history vanishes during review | TTL shorter than human response window | Use appropriate retention and inspect TTL indexes |
| Serialization fails for a client/file object | Resource object was placed in graph state | Store plain data/references; recreate clients as runtime dependencies |
| Old checkpoint fails after deployment | Incompatible graph/state/serializer change | Restore compatible graph version or execute a planned migration |
| DeltaChannel fails with the teaching saver | Explicitly unsupported feature | Use a supported built-in saver or implement its reconstruction contract |
| Notebook says versions differ | Global kernel differs from the course venv | Select/install a kernel with the course requirements |

sections.title: Important version boundaries
sections.body:
- `MemorySaver` is a name encountered in older examples; this course uses
  `InMemorySaver` explicitly.
- Database integrations are separately installable packages. Installing
  `langgraph` alone does not install every saver.
- The custom saver supports ordinary StateGraph channels and explicitly rejects
  DeltaChannel history reconstruction. New optional saver APIs are not assumed
  to be implemented merely because the class inherits a base class.
- Redis key-prefix options were checked in the installed 0.5.2 signatures/source.
  Do not assume an older version accepts them.
- Built-in database tables are implementation details. Let the integration own
  its migrations; use separate tables for business reporting.
- Provider/cloud examples are marked separately from local executed tests.
  Current package signatures are not a substitute for a live integration test.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.body:
Environment: Windows, Python 3.12.9, isolated course environment.
Date: 28 October 2026. Package details are in [SOURCES.md](checkpointers_masterclass/SOURCES.md).

sections.title: Executed locally
sections.body:
- `python labs.py all`: 33 deterministic examples covering state, identity,
  reducers, history, interrupts, failures, SQLite, the custom saver, async,
  composition and serialization.
- `python export_snapshots.py`: three business-table export examples, including
  duplicate-safe re-export and independent thread reporting.
- `python advanced_labs.py all`: six examples covering Functional API task
  recovery/continuity, loops, Send fan-out and parallel review responses.
- `python -m pytest -q`: nine custom-saver behavior tests.
- `restart_demo.py start`, `inspect`, `resume`: separate processes used one
  persistent SQLite file; the final process completed the saved approval.
- `python -m compileall -q .`: Python syntax compilation.
- `python build_notebook.py` and `python verify_course.py`: notebook generation,
  chapter/example counts, local Markdown links and execution of notebook code
  cells through a Python runner that supports top-level await.

The revised notebook is also available directly at
`LangGraph/7_checkpointers_complete.ipynb`. Both copies contain the same inline
Python implementations, with no imports from the companion course modules.
Validation checks those imports and the links from the top-level notebook.

The test suite checks reopened approval, partial parallel failure, preservation
of the original fork history, namespace/filter/pagination behavior, duplicate
and reserved writes, async interoperability, parameter binding, atomic deletion
rollback, and explicit rejection of unsupported delta-history reconstruction.

sections.title: API/source inspected, not live service-tested
sections.body:
PostgreSQL, MongoDB and Redis constructors and relevant installed source were
inspected. The nine service-dependent recipes require explicit environment
variables and an isolated database service. No server credentials were used and
no database service was provisioned during author validation.

Their migrations, live connection behavior, database permissions, Redis module
availability, actual expiry timing and distributed concurrency therefore still
need testing in the target environment.

The Cosmos DB integration is documented from Microsoft's reference. The MySQL,
SQL Server and DynamoDB/object-store designs are implementation blueprints, not
executed or complete database adapters. The optional encryption configuration is
not part of the executed core tests. The notebook was checked by executing its
code cells, not by rendering it in a Jupyter UI.

sections.title: Scope of the custom saver
sections.body:
The custom SQLite saver is suitable for studying the contract and exercising the
ordinary graph channels used here. It has explicit limits documented in chapter
11. These nine tests are meaningful behavior checks, not an exhaustive upstream
conformance suite, performance benchmark or proof of distributed exactly-once
execution.
